tasks.title: Reading a NordGrid Bronze Layer

description.context: Time to put it all together. The senior engineer hands the junior a pointer to NordGrid's actual bronze meter layer. The junior must read the layout — directory structure, partition counts, file sizes — and answer four questions about whether it follows the rules learned in SLJ1-SLJ4. Some things are right; some are wrong; the junior must read carefully.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Real NordGrid bronze layer layout — date+region partitioning with mixed file sizes; 4 questions audit different aspects

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Layout summary (s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/)

# Partition columns: date, region
# Partition count: 1,460 (365 days × 4 regions)
# Total data: 268 GB
# File count: 14,600 (10 files per partition on average)

# Sampled directory listings:

$ ls layout/date=2025-04-30/region=NORTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (12 MB)
  part-00001.parquet  (15 MB)
  part-00002.parquet  (11 MB)
  ... (10 files, each ~12-15 MB)
  Average partition size: 130 MB

$ ls layout/date=2025-04-15/region=SOUTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (180 MB)
  Average partition size: 180 MB

# Catalog metadata
#   Last ANALYZE TABLE: 2 days ago
#   sizeInBytes: 268000000000
#   rowCount: 500_000_000

# Common query pattern observed in production:
#   df.filter((col('date') >= '2025-04-01') & 
#             (col('date') < '2025-05-01') &
#             (col('region') == 'NORTH')).agg(...)
#   ↑ April 2025 NORTH region only — typical monthly report

fields.label: Q1 — What is the partition scheme of this layout?
options: Single-column partitioning by date; the region= subdirectories are file-name suffixes, not partition columns. Spark reads the whole top-level structure for every query.
Bucketing by date and region (not partitioning); the directory names are bucket markers. Bucket count is 1,460 hash-distributed buckets.
No partitioning — the 14,600 files are all at the top level; the date= and region= prefixes are just file-naming conventions, not actual partitioning.
Two-column nested partitioning by date then region. 365 date directories × 4 region directories per date = 1,460 total partitions. The date+region pattern from SLJ4.2.
fields.correctAnswer: Two-column nested partitioning by date then region. 365 date directories × 4 region directories per date = 1,460 total partitions. The date+region pattern from SLJ4.2.
fields.rationale: parquet — two levels of column=value naming means two partition columns.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Misreads region= as a name suffix; it's a separate directory level.

fields.label: Q2 — Looking at date=2025-04-30/region=NORTH/ with 10 files of ~12-15MB each, is there a small-file problem at the partition level?
options: No problem — 10 files per partition is normal Spark output (writes go through 10 shuffle partitions by default). 12-15MB per file is fine for typical workloads.
Mild problem — files are 12-15MB but target is 100-1000MB per file. Per-file overhead times 10 files per partition adds up. The April-15 SOUTH partition (1 file at 180MB) is closer to ideal.
Severe problem — 12-15MB files are catastrophically small. Spark cannot read them at all without first compacting. The pipeline must be halted until OPTIMIZE is run.
No problem — the file size doesn't matter as long as the partition size (130MB) is in the target range. Internal file count is irrelevant to read performance.
fields.correctAnswer: Mild problem — files are 12-15MB but target is 100-1000MB per file. Per-file overhead times 10 files per partition adds up. The April-15 SOUTH partition (1 file at 180MB) is closer to ideal.
fields.rationale: The partition size (130MB) is in the acceptable range, but it's split across 10 files of 12-15MB each.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats 10 small files as fine; per-file overhead is real.
Option C: Overstates the problem; 12MB files are small but readable.

fields.label: Q3 — For the typical query (April 2025 NORTH region), how many partitions will Spark read?
options: All 1,460 partitions; the multi-column filter prevents pruning because Spark cannot evaluate AND conditions at the partition layer.
120 partitions; Spark reads all 30 days of April × 4 regions, then filters region after reading. The region filter applies post-scan.
30 partitions; the April-month range prunes to 30 dates, AND region == NORTH prunes to 1 region per date. 30 × 1 = 30 directories read.
1 partition; Spark consolidates the date range plus region filter into a single partition lookup using bloom filters at the file level instead.
fields.correctAnswer: 30 partitions; the April-month range prunes to 30 dates, AND region == NORTH prunes to 1 region per date. 30 × 1 = 30 directories read.
fields.rationale: Both filters are on partition columns, so both apply at directory-discovery time.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents an AND-blocks-pruning rule that doesn't exist.
Option B: Treats region filter as post-scan; it's a partition column so it prunes.

fields.label: Q4 — At 100× scale (50 billion rows instead of 500 million), would this layout still work?
options: Yes, identically. Storage layout is dataset-size-independent; the same scheme works at any scale because Spark's parallelism scales linearly with cluster size and data.
At 100× scale the layout becomes catastrophic; 1460 partitions × 18GB each exceeds Spark's hard limit on partition size. The dataset must be re-partitioned across more dimensions.

Partition count is unchanged but per-partition file count would explode (14,600 files in one partition each). This creates a within-partition small-file problem; OPTIMIZE/compaction becomes essential.

Partition COUNT will still be appropriate (1460 partitions of ~18GB each). Each partition will be too LARGE — 18GB takes too long to read sequentially. Add a third partition level (date, region, hour) to split.
fields.correctAnswer: Partition COUNT will still be appropriate (1460 partitions of ~18GB each). Each partition will be too LARGE — 18GB takes too long to read sequentially. Add a third partition level (date, region, hour) to split.
fields.rationale: 100× more data with the same partition scheme means each partition holds 100× more data — ~18GB per partition instead of 180MB.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats layout as scale-independent; partition size matters per query.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lessons 3-5 (Pruning, Small File Problem, Partition Column Selection).

tasks.title: Same Data, Two Layouts

description.context: The senior engineer shows the junior two different layouts of the same NordGrid 500K-meter dataset. Layout A partitions by date only (365 directories). Layout B partitions by date AND region (1460 directories). Same source data, same total bytes (~268GB). The senior asks: which layout favors which query patterns, what is the file-count trade-off, and which is the right pick for NordGrid given how queries actually filter? This is the synthesis exercise — every concept from SLJ1-SLJ4 applies.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Same 268GB NordGrid dataset written two ways — date-only partitioning vs date+region partitioning

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Layout A — date only
#   meters.write.partitionBy('date').parquet('layout_a/')

$ ls layout_a/date=2025-04-30/
  part-00000.parquet  (185 MB)
  part-00001.parquet  (180 MB)
  part-00002.parquet  (175 MB)
  part-00003.parquet  (190 MB)
  Average partition size: ~730 MB across 4 files

# Total: 365 partitions, 1460 files (~4 per partition)

# Layout B — date and region
#   meters.write.partitionBy('date', 'region').parquet('layout_b/')

$ ls layout_b/date=2025-04-30/region=NORTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (180 MB)
  Average partition size: ~180 MB (one region's data)

# Total: 1,460 partitions, 1,460 files (1 per partition)

# NordGrid query mix (from production logs):
#   60% queries: filter on date range only (e.g., 'last 7 days')
#   30% queries: filter on date AND region (regional reports)
#   10% queries: filter on region only (rare, full-history)

fields.label: Q1 — For a query filtering only on date ('last 7 days'), which layout reads less data?
options: Layout A reads less. Date-only means 7 partitions × ~730MB = ~5GB. Layout B reads 7 dates × 4 regions = 28 partitions × 180MB = ~5GB. Roughly equal in bytes but Layout A has lower per-directory overhead.
Layout B reads less because more partitions means more pruning opportunities; Spark exploits the extra granularity to skip even within-date partitions through aggressive optimization.
Layout A reads less by 4× because date-only has 4× fewer partitions; partition count drives bytes-read directly regardless of per-partition data size in either layout.

Both layouts read identical bytes for date-only filters. Pruning eliminates non-matching dates equally well in either layout; the within-date file structure is irrelevant for byte-count purposes during the scan.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout A reads less. Date-only means 7 partitions × ~730MB = ~5GB. Layout B reads 7 dates × 4 regions = 28 partitions × 180MB = ~5GB. Roughly equal in bytes but Layout A has lower per-directory overhead.
fields.rationale: For date-only queries, both layouts prune to the same dates.Layout A reads 7 dates × ~730MB = ~5GB across 28 files.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats more partitions as auto-better; benefits only when filter is on the extra column.

fields.label: Q2 — For a query filtering on date AND region, which layout reads less?
options: Layout A reads less because the filter on region is post-scan; Spark reads full date partitions then filters region in memory. Less file overhead than Layout B's deeper directory structure on each query path.

Layout B reads ~4× less. Both filters on partition columns means Layout B prunes to 1 directory per date (matching region only). Layout A reads the full 730MB partition and applies region filter post-scan.
Both layouts read the same bytes for combined filters; the AND condition is evaluated identically by Spark regardless of the underlying partition scheme used at write time.
Layout B reads MORE because nested partitioning forces Spark to do two-level directory listing, which costs extra metadata reads that exceed the byte savings from the additional region-level pruning.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout B reads ~4× less. Both filters on partition columns means Layout B prunes to 1 directory per date (matching region only). Layout A reads the full 730MB partition and applies region filter post-scan.
fields.rationale: This is where Layout B wins decisively.3GB.Layout A can only prune on date; it reads 7 × 730MB = ~5GB and then filters region post-scan.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats post-scan filter as cheap; reading 4× more data costs 4× more time.

fields.label: Q3 — Look at the file count trade-off: 1460 files in Layout A vs 1460 files in Layout B. Same number, very different shapes. What is the implication?
options: File count is identical, so neither layout has a small-file problem. Both are fine; choose based on query patterns alone, since file count is the only relevant metric.
Layout A has more files because 4 files per partition is wasteful. Switch to Layout B regardless of query pattern; fewer files per partition is always better.
Total is identical but per-partition structure diverges. Layout A puts 4 files of ~180MB into each partition. Layout B puts 1 file of ~180MB into each partition. Layout B has cleaner structure.
Layout B has 4× more directories which is a small-file problem at the directory level even though file count is equal. Layout A is preferable for filesystem efficiency.
fields.correctAnswer: Total is identical but per-partition structure diverges. Layout A puts 4 files of ~180MB into each partition. Layout B puts 1 file of ~180MB into each partition. Layout B has cleaner structure.
fields.rationale: Total file count is identical at 1,460 — but the SHAPE differs.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats per-partition file count as irrelevant when total is OK.
Option B: Treats Layout B as universally better; query pattern matters.

fields.label: Q4 — Given NordGrid's actual query mix (60% date-only, 30% date+region, 10% region-only), which layout is the right pick and why?
options: Layout A wins because 60% of queries are date-only, and Layout A is slightly faster on those due to fewer per-directory listings. The 30% combined queries pay a cost but it's tolerable.
Both layouts perform equivalently in production due to caching and AQE optimizations applied automatically. Pick whichever based on team preference; performance is unaffected by the choice.

Layout B wins because the 30% combined queries get 4× speedup, the 10% region-only queries get pruning Layout A cannot offer, and 60% date-only queries are roughly equal. Net: B is better or equal on every class.
Neither is right; the correct layout for this mix is partitionBy('region', 'date') — region first because it has lower cardinality. Layout B's column ordering is reversed and that is the issue.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout B wins because the 30% combined queries get 4× speedup, the 10% region-only queries get pruning Layout A cannot offer, and 60% date-only queries are roughly equal. Net: B is better or equal on every class.
fields.rationale: Weighted analysis: 60% date-only ≈ tied between layouts, 30% combined gets 4× speedup with Layout B, 10% region-only gets pruning in Layout B (Layout.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Optimizes for the majority pattern at the cost of significant minority gains.
